name: GHK-Cu
used_for: Mainly an ingredient in cosmetic skin and hair products, promoted for wrinkles, skin firmness, wound and scar appearance and hair thickness. The evidence is largely cosmetic, topical, in vitro or in animals; there are very few controlled human trials, and injectable use is promoted online without an approved product or established human evidence.

entries.text: Animal study only, not human data: 0.3 or 3 mg/ml GHK-Cu was injected into the knee joint once a week for 4 weeks (from week 2 after surgery) in a rat model of ACL reconstruction.

Animal study only, not human data: GHK (without copper) was injected into the abdominal cavity every other day at 2.6, 26 or 260 micrograms per day (as reported) from day 4 to day 21 after bleomycin lung injury.

internet_entries.text: A clinic website says injectable GHK-Cu is most commonly dosed at 1 to 2 mg per day subcutaneously, and topical GHK-Cu at 2 to 4 percent once or twice daily.
internet_entries.population: As described by the source, not a study population

administration_guidance.text: A peptide information site that also sells or links to suppliers says GHK-Cu is used either as a topical cream or serum applied once or twice daily, or as a subcutaneous injection of reconstituted powder rotated across the abdomen, outer thigh and back of the upper arm. It says the mixed vial is kept refrigerated and protected from light, used within the supplier's stated window, and discarded if cloudy or containing particles. It gives no preferred time of day.
administration_guidance.label: internet

administration_guidance.text: A medical spa chain's marketing guide says many providers favor evening or bedtime injection on the rationale that tissue repair is concentrated during sleep, that a mixed vial is refrigerated and used within roughly 28 to 30 days, and that topical products are often the evidence-based starting point for facial anti-aging.
administration_guidance.label: internet

side_effects.text: A peptide information site that also sells or links to suppliers says topical GHK-Cu can cause redness, tingling, dryness or transient irritation, especially at higher concentrations, and that injected use can cause local redness, mild swelling, transient warmth or a bluish bruise attributed to the copper complex.
side_effects.label: internet

internet_claims.claim: A medical clinic's blog says GHK-Cu boosts collagen and elasticity, reduces wrinkles and may support hair growth and thickness, while conceding more studies are needed for the hair claims; the clinic itself offers GHK-Cu serums, a scalp solution and injections.

A dermatology practice says online marketing overstates copper peptides (for example that they outperform retinoids), and that research supports gradual benefits such as collagen support and wound healing, not dramatic results or replacement of retinoids.

research.summary: Small randomized trial (Arch Facial Plast Surg) of skin care products with or without GHK-Cu after CO2 laser resurfacing around the mouth; 13 patients completed it.
research.finding: Blinded objective measures showed no significant difference between groups in redness resolution, wrinkles or skin quality. Patients using GHK-Cu rated overall skin quality higher on a questionnaire. Very small and a cosmetic product setting.

research.summary: Cell-culture study (Arch Facial Plast Surg) of copper tripeptide and tretinoin on normal and keloid-producing human dermal fibroblasts.
research.finding: Copper tripeptide lowered secretion of TGF-beta1 in keloid-producing fibroblasts at 24 hours (a similar trend in normal fibroblasts). Cell culture only; it does not show clinical benefit for scars.

research.summary: Rat study (J Orthop Res) of weekly intra-articular GHK-Cu injections after ACL reconstruction (72 rats, saline versus two doses).
research.finding: Knee laxity was better at 6 weeks and graft stiffness higher at the lower dose, but no significant differences were seen at 12 weeks or in several other measures. The authors concluded the benefit was transient.

research.summary: Mouse and cell study (Wound Repair Regen) of GHK-Cu encapsulated in liposomes for scald wounds.
research.finding: Liposomal GHK-Cu increased blood-vessel cell growth in culture and shortened scald wound healing to 14 days in mice compared with free GHK-Cu. A special formulation in animals, not human evidence.

research.summary: Mouse study (Front Pharmacol) of GHK peptide (not the copper complex) in bleomycin-induced lung fibrosis.
research.finding: GHK reduced inflammation and fibrosis markers in the mice. Animal data only and a different compound form than cosmetic GHK-Cu.

research.summary: FDA web page on bulk drug substances for compounding that may present significant safety risks (page dated 04/22/2026, fetched 2026-09-30).
research.finding: On the fetched page GHK-Cu (copper peptide) appears in the table of bulk drug substances nominated but later withdrawn, with FDA noting that compounded injectable drugs containing GHK-Cu may pose a risk of immunogenicity due to the potential for aggregation. The page does not describe an approved product.

research.summary: Narrative review (Biomed Res Int) by Pickart, Vasquez-Soltero and Margolina, whose listed affiliation is a skin-care research and development company, on GHK in skin regeneration.
research.finding: Describes GHK as a plasma peptide that declines with age, proposed to act with copper to stimulate collagen and repair. Reports 12-week cosmetic cream studies in women with sun-damaged skin (for example 67 women, applied twice daily) with improved firmness and fewer fine lines, and calls cosmetic use very safe. Authors are not independent and the cream strength is not stated.

research.summary: Narrative review (Int J Mol Sci) by Pickart and Margolina, with the same skin-care company affiliation, on regenerative and protective actions of GHK-Cu in light of gene-expression data.
research.finding: Summarizes lab, animal and gene-expression data suggesting GHK stimulates blood vessel and nerve outgrowth, collagen and tissue repair, with anti-inflammatory actions. Mostly not human clinical evidence. Abstract read; full text not accessed.

dose.summary: No dose has been established for any route, and there is no approved product. Cosmetic creams were studied for 12 weeks without a stated strength in the review found, and the only injection doses come from rat and mouse studies. Online sources describe injections of about 1 to 3 mg a day and creams of 1 to 4 percent, none of it tested in people. Oral GHK-Cu has no good human data.

items.text: Review of cosmetic use (Pickart and colleagues, authors affiliated with a skin-care company): facial and eye cream studies in women with sun-damaged skin lasted 12 weeks. One study of 67 women used the cream twice daily. The review does not state the cream strength.

mechanism.summary: GHK is a small peptide found naturally in human blood that declines with age. It is proposed to work as a copper complex that boosts collagen and drives tissue repair, but this comes mostly from lab and animal work, and how it acts in people is not established.

items.text: Review (Pickart and colleagues, authors affiliated with a skin-care company): GHK is present in human plasma, saliva and urine and declines with age, is proposed to act as a complex with copper, stimulates collagen and other skin matrix molecules, and attracts immune and endothelial cells to injuries. Most of the evidence described is from cells and animals.
items.label: research

items.text: Review (Pickart and Margolina): GHK is described as stimulating blood vessel and nerve outgrowth and collagen, elastin and glycosaminoglycan production, with anti-inflammatory and tissue-repair actions drawn largely from lab and animal studies and gene-expression data.
items.label: research

items.text: Cell-culture study of copper tripeptide on normal and keloid-producing human skin fibroblasts: it lowered secretion of the signaling protein TGF-beta1 in keloid-producing cells at 24 hours.
items.label: research

best_documented_effect.summary: No strong human evidence. The one small randomized trial found no objective benefit after laser resurfacing, and company-linked cosmetic studies report gentler skin changes over 12 weeks. A dermatologist warns that online claims are overstated.

items.text: Randomized trial of skin care products with or without GHK-Cu after CO2 laser resurfacing (13 patients completed): blinded objective measures showed no significant difference, though patients rated overall skin quality higher with GHK-Cu.
items.label: research

side_effect_groups.title: Topical
side_effect_groups.summary: Redness, tingling, dryness or irritation, mostly at higher strengths. A review by company-linked authors calls cosmetic use very safe.

items.text: Review (authors affiliated with a skin-care company) says no issues have arisen in use as a skin cosmetic or in human wound-healing studies.
items.label: research

items.text: A peptide information site that also sells or links to suppliers says topical GHK-Cu can cause redness, tingling, dryness or transient irritation, especially at higher concentrations.
items.label: internet

items.text: Westlake Dermatology says copper peptides can cause skin irritation or redness, especially at higher concentrations, and tingling in reactive skin, and to reduce frequency or stop if skin becomes irritated.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Injected
side_effect_groups.summary: Online sources describe local redness, swelling, warmth and bruising, and sometimes mild nausea. No human safety trial of injected GHK-Cu was found.

items.text: A peptide information site that also sells or links to suppliers says injected use can cause local redness, mild swelling, transient warmth or a bluish bruise attributed to the copper complex.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptidesExplorer says injection site redness and warmth resolve within an hour, with mild bruising, and that nausea is rare and typically dose-dependent.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Grades, a vendor-ranking site that links to sellers, says user accounts commonly describe stinging or burning at the injection site, redness or slight swelling, mild nausea and temporary flushing.
items.label: internet

items.text: The Peptide Guides, a site that links to vendors, says injection-site redness, itching or swelling is most common, with rare transient nausea or headache, and lists abdominal pain, nausea and a metallic taste as signs of copper toxicity it calls unlikely.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Regulator warning
side_effect_groups.summary: The FDA says compounded injectable GHK-Cu may carry a risk of immune reactions.

items.text: FDA page on bulk drug substances for compounding (dated 04/22/2026) lists GHK-Cu among substances nominated and later withdrawn, and says compounded injectable drugs containing GHK-Cu may pose risk for immunogenicity due to the potential for aggregation and peptide-related impurities.
items.label: research

side_effect_groups.title: Oral
side_effect_groups.summary: Online sources say oral use is poorly absorbed and not well studied, and long-term effects are unknown.

items.text: InCare, a Florida medical clinic that offers peptide therapy consultations, says long-term effects of oral GHK-Cu remain unknown, there is very limited human data, and no oral GHK-Cu product has FDA approval.
items.label: internet
